extracted.intended_audience: law students, patent practitioners, and inventors seeking legal guidance on entitlement and renewal rules
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and doctrinal criteria about who may take a patent, how inventions must be claimed (sole vs joint), the limits on multiple patents, the rights of aliens, administrators and assignees, and the statutory procedure and substantive standards for obtaining extensions/renewals of patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of subject-matter / aggregation of improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate machines or improvements that conduce to the same general end may be united in one patent as distinct improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If each machine is new, they may be united in one patent; where the patent is for them conjointly, infringement of any one of the invented machines or improvements is sufficient to violate the patent (i.e., a wrongful use of one device 'fro tanto' violates the conjoint patent). This doctrine follows Moody v. Fiske and related authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Must claim invention as sole or joint accurately
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject-matter should be claimed as the sole invention of one party if that is the fact, or as the joint invention of two or more parties if it was invented by more than one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A joint invention may be the subject of a patent and the statute provides for it; but if an invention made by more than one person is patented by any one of them as sole and that person takes the oath declaring himself original and first inventor, the patent will be void. Conversely, a joint patent for a true sole invention encounters the same objection.

rubrics_metrics.name: No two subsisting patents for the same invention
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor cannot have two subsisting valid patents at the same time for the same invention; the first patent is an estoppel to any subsequent patent by the same person for the same invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holding both sole and joint patents (or multiple patents) for the same invention is inconsistent and may be voided to prevent double recovery and to avoid prolonging exclusivity beyond the statutory term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee must be original and first inventor (persons entitled)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only the inventor or inventors of the thing proposed to be patented may receive a patent; the patentee must be the original and first inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute does not permit patents merely for introduction of an invention from abroad; entitlement is grounded in being the original/first inventor. Related procedural requirements (oath/affirmation of original invention) enforce this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executor/administrator may apply if inventor died
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the inventor has died before applying, the right to apply for and obtain a patent devolves on his executor or administrator, in trust for his heirs or devisees; the required oath/affirmation is varied accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An administrator is competent to apply for and receive extensions as well (see extension provisions), and statutes contemplate this contingency explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights of aliens to obtain patents in U.S.
rubrics_metrics.description: An alien who is the first and original inventor may apply for and obtain a U.S. patent in the same manner as a U.S. citizen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory provisions address foreign patents/publications: earlier law provided a six-month window from foreign patent/publication; later amendments (Act of 1839) allowed a foreign patent more than six months prior to not bar a U.S. patent provided the invention has not been introduced into public and common use in the United States prior to the U.S. application. The patent office treats the date of enrolment of a foreign patent as its operative date for priority in interfering applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory procedure for extension/renewal (§18 of Act of 1836)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee (not an assignee) desiring an extension beyond the term of limitation may apply to the commissioner, setting forth grounds, and must provide specified notices; a board (secretary of state, commissioner, solicitor of the treasury) is constituted to hear evidence for and against the extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patentee is required to furnish a sworn statement showing the ascertained value of the invention and receipts/expenditures sufficient to exhibit true account of loss and profit. The board must be 'to the full and entire satisfaction' having due regard to public interest that it is just and proper to extend because the patentee, without neglect or fault, failed to attain reasonable remuneration for his time, ingenuity, and expense in introducing the invention into use. No extension shall be granted after expiration of the original term; applications must be made while the original patent is running.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrator may receive extension even if patentee had disposed interest
rubrics_metrics.description: An administrator is competent to apply for and receive an extension although the patentee had disposed of all his interest in the then existing patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The courts have held administrators can be grantees of renewal certificates under the statute, but other doctrines (see assignee-benefit rules) affect who benefits from the renewal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renewal generally benefits inventor, not assignees (no automatic inurement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The extension does not automatically inure to the benefit of assignees under the original patent unless such right is expressly conveyed by the patentee; the renewal is intended for the inventor (patentee).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Majority Supreme Court rule: extension does not enure to assignees under original patent but to the administrator when granted to an administrator; however, assignees who were using the patented machine at the time of renewal retain a right to use it, though not to make and sell it. The 18th section's clause extending benefit 'to assignees and grantees... to the extent of their respective interest therein' must be read in light of common law principles — assignees get no more than the interest the assignor had power to grant at the time, unless the assignment expressly or necessarily implies broader rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignments/licenses limited to what existed at time of conveyance
rubrics_metrics.description: A grant or assignment conveys only what the grantor/assignor then possessed (actual or potential); it cannot at law pass a mere future possibility unless expressed as a covenant or contract enforceable in equity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a grant/assignment purportedly covers rights not then in existence (e.g., future renewals), the remedy for the assignee is generally equitable (specific enforcement of covenant) unless the instrument clearly shows an intention to include future-created rights. Courts construe renewal-benefit clauses so as not to deprive inventor of statutory bounty unless the parties clearly intended otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive rule: 'benefit of renewal extends to assignees to extent of their interest'
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutory clause protecting assignees/grantees by extending benefit 'to the extent of their respective interest therein' limits protection to the extent of the interest actually conveyed under the original patent, not to enlarge their rights beyond original terms unless language implies broader intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the original assignment was limited to the original term, assignees will not have benefit beyond that term; if the assignment expressly or necessarily conveys contingent/future interests (e.g., rights in a renewed patent), then the clause protects that interest. Courts balance statutory intent to reward inventors against protections for assignees who paid for prospective benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing/priority rule for foreign patents in interference
rubrics_metrics.description: In interfering applications between an alien and a U.S. citizen, the date of enrolment (not sealing) of the foreign patent is considered by the patent office as the operative foreign-patent date for priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This date limits how far back the foreign applicant may go to prove priority of invention in the U.S. proceeding.
